strengths: Addresses an important problem: training-free uncertainty estimation for large vision-language models, with potential value for calibration and data acquisition.
The combination of last-layer Laplace approximations, analytic uncertainty propagation, and active learning is intuitively appealing and computationally motivated.
Experiments cover two VLM families, several classification datasets, cross-domain active learning, multiple model sizes, and both calibration and predictive-performance metrics.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes substantial derivational and experimental detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central cosine-similarity derivation is mathematically invalid. Equation (56) replaces the expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations even though the numerator and random norms are dependent. The variance derivation repeats this unsupported denominator substitution. Consequently, Equations (59) and (65) are heuristics rather than derived moments, undermining the paper's main claim of principled analytic uncertainty propagation.

The assumed diagonal embedding covariance is not justified and conflicts with Equation (9), whose covariance is proportional to the generally dense inverse Kronecker factor. Discarding these correlations can materially affect both cosine moments and uncertainty estimates.

Figures 3 and 5 report quantities called cosine similarities with values extending roughly from -10 to 30, although cosine similarity must lie in [-1,1]. These may instead be temperature-scaled logits, but that transformation is absent from the stated derivation and captions, exposing a major mismatch between the theory and experiments.

Other technical formulas are also problematic or inconsistent. The marginal-likelihood expression in Equations (27)-(28) subtracts products of determinants rather than log determinants and omits essential terms. The factorized incorporation of an isotropic prior introduces unmotivated cross terms. The appendix reverses the sign of BALD in Equation (72), while online curvature updates differ between the main paper and appendix by using n+t versus sqrt(n+t). These issues make the implemented method impossible to infer reliably.

The approximation-quality evidence is inadequate: it uses only 500 synthetic samples and a qualitative KDE plot, with no quantitative error, coverage, tail behavior, sensitivity to covariance structure, or comparison against direct posterior Monte Carlo on real data. Thus, the central approximation is not validated under realistic conditions.

The zero-shot comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. PCME++ uses a different ViT-B/16 checkpoint and different training data than the OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 model, producing drastically lower accuracy and making the comparison difficult to interpret. Strong post-hoc UQ baselines, ensembles, and direct Monte Carlo propagation of the same Laplace posterior are missing. Improvements over temperature scaling are also small or mixed on multiple datasets.

The active-learning evidence lacks numerical tables, uncertainty across independent acquisition and fine-tuning runs, and clear significance testing. Curves are visibly noisy, while per-domain validation is used to select checkpoints and EPIG hyperparameters. The method also uses the unlabeled test inputs transductively, so the conclusions do not directly establish performance in standard pool-based active learning.

Reproducibility is compromised by conflicting Hessian sample counts (30,000 in the main text versus 327,680 in the appendix), missing implementation details for predictive propagation and Monte Carlo acquisition, inconsistent equations, and an empty code-availability statement. Given that the reported empirical behavior cannot resolve the central theoretical errors, the main claims are not adequately supported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: obtaining uncertainty estimates from pretrained vision-language models without retraining the full model or adding a learned uncertainty adapter.
Combining last-layer Laplace approximations with probabilistic cosine similarities is intuitively appealing and potentially useful for both calibration and data acquisition.

The evaluation covers two VLM families, several zero-shot datasets, cross-domain active learning, and multiple model sizes. The reported CLIP calibration results are generally favorable, although often modest.
The manuscript is organized clearly and includes substantial derivational and experimental detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central cosine-similarity derivation is not mathematically valid as written. Equation (56) equates the expectation of a ratio with a ratio of expectations, even though the numerator and random norms are dependent. The variance derivation makes the same substitution. These formulas are therefore heuristics rather than the claimed analytical moment calculation, and their accuracy is supported only by one small synthetic-style experiment with 500 samples.

The marginal-likelihood expression in Equations (27)-(28) is incorrect or severely underspecified: it subtracts products of Hessian determinants directly from a log likelihood, rather than including the log prior and log-determinant terms of a Laplace marginal likelihood. Since marginal-likelihood optimization determines the prior precision, this undermines a central implementation step unless it is merely a presentation error.

Other technical inconsistencies reduce confidence: the appendix reverses the sign of BALD in Equation (72), the KFAC-plus-prior expression introduces unexplained cross terms relative to H+lambda I, full feature covariances are reduced to diagonal form without justification, and Equation (24) applies the image encoder notation to text inputs.

The empirical gains do not convincingly isolate the proposed uncertainty model. Against temperature-scaled CLIP, BayesVLM is worse on some dataset/metric combinations and tied on others. For SigLIP, improvements over the uncalibrated model are tiny or negative on several datasets, while the temperature-scaling baseline catastrophically degrades ECE to 46-66%, suggesting an incorrect or poorly configured baseline.
The PCME++ comparison is confounded by using a different backbone/checkpoint and training data; its very large accuracy deficit makes it an uninformative baseline for the main claim.

The active-learning evaluation lacks error bars, results across independent selection/training runs, or statistical tests. It compares mainly with random and entropy acquisition, omitting stronger contemporary active-learning and diversity-based baselines. Hyperparameters and stopping checkpoints are selected using domain-specific validation data, further weakening the evidential value of small curve differences.

There are important reproducibility contradictions: the main text says the Hessian uses 30,000 LAION pairs, whereas the appendix says 327,680. The paper ends with an empty code-availability statement, and key details such as prompts, calibration-bin settings, Monte Carlo budgets, acquisition computation costs, and run counts are missing.

The method is less generally post-hoc and training-free than advertised: it requires hundreds of thousands of pretraining-like image-text pairs, curvature estimation with automatic differentiation, and labeled proxy data for tuning the pseudo-data count. Its acknowledged failure mode under pretraining-data mismatch is particularly relevant because original training data are unavailable for many VLMs.

Claims about interpretability and out-of-distribution uncertainty rest on a single randomly selected example with artificial character and square corruptions. This is inadequate to establish either claim, especially for the safety-critical applications invoked by the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: obtaining uncertainty estimates from pretrained vision-language models without retraining the full model or modifying its architecture.

BayesVLM presents a coherent pipeline combining a last-layer Laplace approximation, efficient uncertainty propagation, and Bayesian active-learning acquisition functions. The analytical treatment makes inference substantially more practical than repeated parameter sampling.

The evaluation covers two VLM families, five zero-shot classification datasets, cross-domain active learning on OfficeHome, and two ImageNet variants. The active-learning results are generally encouraging, especially for CLIP-Huge.
The paper is clearly organized, motivates the method well, includes substantial derivational detail, and explicitly discusses the limitation caused by unavailable pretraining data.
The use of both calibration metrics and downstream active-learning performance is valuable: it tests whether the estimated uncertainty is operationally useful rather than reporting calibration alone.
weaknesses: The central cosine-similarity derivation is not an exact moment calculation. In particular, Eq. (56) replaces the expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations, while Eqs. (62–65) similarly treat the random normalization terms as deterministic. These are uncontrolled approximations, yet the resulting expressions are sometimes presented as the expected value and variance. The additional diagonal-covariance assumption discards correlations present in the KFAC posterior without adequate justification.

Validation of the cosine approximation is weak for a central technical contribution: it consists mainly of one qualitative density plot using 500 samples. A quantitative error study across posterior scales, embedding dimensions, covariance structures, and real image-text pairs—and comparisons with Monte Carlo or delta-method alternatives—is needed.

The zero-shot gains over a properly tuned calibration baseline are modest and inconsistent. For CLIP, temperature scaling matches or exceeds BayesVLM on several NLPD/ECE entries; for SigLIP, improvements over the uncalibrated model are often negligible and ECE worsens on Flowers-102 and Food-101. The extremely poor SigLIP temperature-scaling results also warrant investigation and make that comparison unconvincing.

The active-learning figures lack error bars, results across independent selection/training seeds, and statistical tests. Consequently, it is difficult to determine whether several apparent gains are robust. Comparisons with stronger diversity-aware, coreset, and recent VLM-specific active-learning methods are also missing.

The method's advertised post-hoc applicability is constrained by its reliance on pretraining data and loss information for Hessian estimation. The acknowledged CLIP/SigLIP data mismatch illustrates that this is a material practical limitation, but there is no systematic proxy-data sensitivity study.

There are reproducibility inconsistencies: the main text reports using 30k LAION pairs whereas the supplement reports 327,680, and the stated pseudo-data-count search ranges also differ. Moreover, the reproducibility section says code is available but provides no visible link.

Overall, the idea is promising and the paper has meaningful positive evidence, but the unsupported moment approximation and incomplete experimental validation leave the central claims slightly below the standard required for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: adding epistemic uncertainty to large pretrained vision-language models without retraining or architectural modification.

Combining a last-layer KFAC Laplace approximation with analytic uncertainty propagation is a useful and reasonably novel framework. The method is model-agnostic in principle and has very low reported inference overhead.
The empirical scope is broad: experiments cover multiple CLIP sizes, SigLIP, seven zero-shot datasets, probabilistic embedding models, and active-learning tasks on OfficeHome and ImageNet variants.

BayesVLM generally improves NLPD and ECE over deterministic models, temperature scaling, and test-time adaptation, while largely preserving accuracy. The active-learning results also suggest that its uncertainties have downstream utility.
The paper is well organized and includes algorithms, derivations, computational-cost measurements, and several relevant ablations.
weaknesses: The central ProbCosine derivation is insufficiently justified. Equation (7) replaces an expectation of a ratio with a ratio involving expected squared norms, while the cited triangle inequality only supplies a bound on an expected norm and does not establish the stated approximation. Equation (8) similarly treats the normalization terms as effectively deterministic and omits their covariance with the numerator. No error bound or regime of validity is provided.

The Gaussian approximation is structurally inconsistent with cosine similarity's bounded support. The only approximation-quality study is qualitative, uses merely 500 samples and a fixed KDE bandwidth, reports no numerical divergence or moment error, and even plots values labeled as cosine similarities far outside [-1,1]. This does not adequately validate the paper's main analytic contribution.

The uncertainty baselines are limited. Despite discussing ensembles, dropout, adapters, and probabilistic VLM approaches, the main BayesVLM comparison is primarily against temperature scaling and one test-time adaptation method. Temperature scaling is a weak epistemic-uncertainty baseline and cannot change accuracy, making some comparisons less informative.

The claimed training-free post-hoc applicability is qualified by substantial data and tuning requirements: Hessian estimation uses 327,680 LAION samples, and the pseudo-data count is selected using labeled ImageNet validation NLPD. Performance with a mismatched proxy dataset is inconsistent for SigLIP, yet this is the practically important setting for closed-source pretraining data.

The active-learning evidence lacks uncertainty estimates over repeated acquisition and fine-tuning runs. Curves have no error bars, and conclusions rely on visually small or inconsistent differences on some tasks. Hyperparameters and the reported checkpoint are selected using domain-specific validation data, further weakening the evidence for robust acquisition gains.

The Hessian-sample ablation examines only convergence of the Hessian trace, which does not demonstrate convergence of its spectrum, inverse, predictive covariance, or downstream calibration. Other important assumptions—last-layer-only uncertainty, independence of image and text projections, diagonal embedding covariance, and sensitivity to prior precision—are not adequately ablated.

Claims concerning domain shift and safety-critical use are stronger than the evidence: evaluation focuses on classification calibration and transductive active learning, without standard OOD-detection, selective-prediction, or failure-detection benchmarks. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the central approximation and evaluation need stronger validation for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: obtaining epistemic uncertainty estimates from pretrained vision-language models without full retraining.
Applying a last-layer KFAC Laplace approximation to both image and text projections is computationally pragmatic, and the reported inference overhead is small.
The evaluation covers multiple VLM architectures, classification datasets, calibration metrics, and an active-learning application.
The paper is generally well organized and includes useful implementation details, supplementary derivations, runtime measurements, and some ablations.
weaknesses: The central ProbCosine derivation is not technically justified. Equation (52) incorrectly equates the expectation of a ratio with a ratio of expectations, and the subsequent variance derivation similarly replaces random normalization terms without a principled approximation argument, error bound, or adequate quantitative validation.

The probabilistic embeddings in Equation (19) generally have dense covariance through the inverse Kronecker factor, whereas ProbCosine assumes diagonal covariance. The transition between these settings is not explained, and the effect of discarding correlations is not ablated.

The approximation-quality experiment is inadequate and internally questionable: Figure 9 labels values far outside the valid [-1,1] range as cosine similarities, uses only a qualitative plot for synthetically shifted means, and reports no approximation-error metric across realistic embeddings or uncertainty regimes.

Several headline claims contradict the tables. In Table 2, BayesVLM reduces accuracy on multiple datasets relative to CLIP; in Table 3, ProbCosine worsens accuracy, NLPD, or ECE on several datasets despite the claim of consistent improvement across benchmarks and metrics. SigLIP results are also mixed and frequently worse than the unmodified model.

The calibration comparison is too narrow. The principal competitive baseline is temperature scaling, while relevant modern VLM calibration, probabilistic-adapter, ensemble, and alternative post-hoc uncertainty methods discussed in the paper are not evaluated. Table 1 is not a substitute for empirical comparisons.

The active-learning evidence lacks essential rigor: the number of random seeds and uncertainty intervals are not clearly reported, statistical significance is absent, and extensive domain-specific validation and hyperparameter searches may advantage the proposed acquisition procedures. Using the entire unlabeled test/query set for targeted selection also makes this a transductive setting whose practical assumptions need clearer discussion.

The BALD definition is inconsistent: the entropy difference in Appendix Equation (68) has the opposite sign from standard BALD and from the main-text definition. This creates ambiguity about the implemented acquisition score and undermines reproducibility.

The claim of being broadly model-agnostic is overstated because the approach assumes accessible linear projection layers, compatible training losses, gradients for Hessian estimation, and representative pretraining or proxy data. The proxy-data results on SigLIP show that this dependence is consequential.

The statistical reporting is weak: standard errors appear to be computed over test examples rather than independent training or method runs, the paired t-test protocol is insufficiently specified, and bolded tiny differences do not establish robust method-level improvements.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript states that code is available but provides no actual link, and important details about active-learning repetitions, acquisition computation, prompt construction, ECE binning, and exact statistical units are missing.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: efficient post-hoc uncertainty quantification for pretrained vision-language models, with a coherent connection to active learning.
The last-layer Laplace approach is practically appealing and incurs very little reported inference overhead: below 5% for base models and below 1% for the huge model, with nearly unchanged FLOPs.
Evaluation spans multiple CLIP sizes, SigLIP, seven zero-shot datasets, and cross-domain active-learning tasks. The CLIP experiments show substantial ECE improvements on several datasets.
The paper is polished and generally easy to follow, with useful runtime studies, Hessian sample-size analysis, distance-metric ablations, and a candid discussion of proxy-data limitations.
weaknesses: The central ProbCosine derivation is not mathematically justified. Equation 52 replaces the expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations, and Equation 58 similarly treats random norm terms as deterministic. The upper bound on the expected norm does not validate these substitutions, so the claimed moment formulas and resulting Gaussian distribution do not follow from the stated assumptions.

Equation 6 yields a generally full covariance proportional to the inverse KFAC output factor, whereas ProbCosine abruptly assumes diagonal covariance without explaining or evaluating this additional approximation.

Validation of ProbCosine's approximation quality is inadequate: it is limited to a qualitative synthetic plot with no quantitative error against Monte Carlo moments or densities on realistic embeddings. Moreover, a Gaussian has unbounded support despite cosine similarity being restricted to [-1,1], and Figure 9 appears to display values far outside that range.

The reported marginal-likelihood expression in Equation 24 appears incorrect and dimensionally problematic: it uses a product of determinants rather than the required log-determinant structure and omits important prior and normalization terms. This is especially consequential because the method uses this objective to select the prior precision.

Several empirical claims are overstated. BayesVLM does not consistently improve accuracy in Table 2, SigLIP results are mixed, and ProbCosine worsens ProLIP ECE on multiple datasets. Comparisons are also limited mainly to vanilla models, temperature scaling, and one test-time adaptation method despite discussing ensembles, dropout, and probabilistic adapters.

The active-learning evidence does not cleanly isolate the benefit of the uncertainty estimator. It combines uncertainty scoring, targeted nearest-neighbor selection, online adaptation, and domain-specific hyperparameter tuning; results lack sufficiently clear numerical summaries and variability across independent selection/training runs. Access to the unlabeled test set also makes the setting transductive and narrows the applicability of the conclusions.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code-availability statement has no link, and standard errors over test examples do not capture variability from Hessian subsets, active-learning selection, or fine-tuning. The broad 'training-free' and 'model-agnostic' framing also understates the need for model internals, the original loss, and 327k pretraining or proxy examples. Overall, the promising empirical heuristic does not overcome the unresolved soundness issues in the central technical contribution.
